name: Eggs (egg yolk)

lead: Whole eggs and yolks are a bodybuilding staple, eaten as cheap, complete protein with fat and choline to support muscle gain and a better physique.

The chain runs through overall intake: egg protein scores the maximum on the PDCAAS protein-quality scale, and a hard-boiled egg provides roughly 12.6 g of protein and 294 mg of choline per 100 g. That protein feeds muscle repair and growth alongside training. No published trials were found testing egg yolk specifically for skin, hair or other appearance outcomes.

paras: People eat several eggs a day, boiled, scrambled or in omelettes, mixed into meals for protein and calories during bulks or cuts. Cooked egg protein is more bioavailable than raw.

Research on dietary cholesterol is mixed, and several meta-analyses found no association between moderate egg intake and heart disease in the general population. Raw eggs carry a salmonella risk, and egg allergy is common in infants.

angle.text: Eggs and yolks are a staple of bodybuilding and appearance diets as a cheap, complete protein with fat and choline, supporting muscle gain. The protein feeds muscle repair and growth when paired with training and enough calories. Egg protein quality is well documented.

lead: Whole eggs and egg yolks are a staple of physique-focused eating. People in lifting and looksmaxxing communities use them as an inexpensive, calorie-dense source of complete protein, fat and choline to support muscle gain and a fuller, leaner-looking physique. A hard-boiled chicken egg provides roughly 12.6 g of protein and 294 mg of choline per 100 g, and egg protein scores the maximum on the PDCAAS protein-quality scale.[1]

Forum users on looksmax.org and T Nation describe eating anywhere from a few to well over a dozen eggs a day, cooked or raw, as part of bulking, high-protein or 'animal-based' diets.[2][3][4] Some report more energy the day after eating them, while others compare them unfavourably with chicken as a protein source per calorie.[2][5]

Research on eggs falls mostly into cardiovascular, muscle-protein and weight-control topics. A 2020 BMJ analysis of three large US cohorts and a meta-analysis found that eating at least one egg a day was not associated with incident cardiovascular disease in the general population,[6] and a randomized trial in young men compared whole eggs with egg whites for stimulating muscle protein synthesis after exercise.[7]

paras: Per 100 g, a hard-boiled chicken egg contains about 155 kcal, 10.6 g fat and 1.12 g carbohydrate, along with vitamin B12, riboflavin, vitamin D, vitamin A, phosphorus and choline.[1] The yolk holds most of the fat and the choline, while the white is mostly water and protein.[1]

A systematic review of 141 studies on plant-based and meat-eating diets noted that eggs, dairy, poultry and fish are among the foods that supply nutrients such as vitamin B12, which was generally lower in vegetarians and vegans.[8]

sections.h: Use in training and physique diets
paras: Lifters often count eggs as a cheap way to add protein and fat. A randomized trial in young men reported that whole eggs stimulated post-exercise muscle protein synthesis more than an equal amount of protein from egg whites alone, a result often cited by yolk-eating lifters.[7] A separate multicenter trial in the International Journal of Obesity examined an egg breakfast in a weight-loss setting.[9]

In the T Nation forum, members posting training logs describe days built around many whole eggs and extra yolks alongside meat and shrimp.[10] Others discuss yolks in relation to insulin response and training energy.[11]

Studies of egg intake and heart disease have been inconsistent. A 2013 meta-analysis found no link to heart disease or stroke, while another that year reported modestly higher risk, and a 2018 review of randomized trials found eggs raised LDL and HDL cholesterol compared with no eggs, though not compared with low-egg diets.[1] Two 2020 meta-analyses and an umbrella review found no association between moderate intake and cardiovascular risk in the general population.[1]

The 2020 BMJ analysis pooled participants from the Nurses' Health Study, Nurses' Health Study II and Health Professionals Follow-Up Study, with up to 32 years of follow-up, and reported that at least one egg per day was not associated with incident cardiovascular disease.[6] Its authors noted that higher egg eaters also tended to have higher BMI and eat more red meat.[6]

A 2025 randomized cross-over trial of 61 adults examined the separate effects of dietary cholesterol from eggs and of saturated fat on LDL cholesterol, motivated by recent suggestions that saturated fat has the larger influence.[12] A 2023 meta-analysis of prospective studies associated swapping eggs for nuts with lower cardiovascular risk.[13]

Salmonella can contaminate eggs; a USDA study cited by Wikipedia estimated about 1 in 30,000 US eggs was affected, and cooking to 71 C kills the bacteria.[1] Raw egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable versus about 91 percent for cooked.[1] A food-microbiology study modelled Salmonella growth in unpasteurized liquid whole egg, yolk and white.[14]

Raw-egg drinking is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, with threads asking whether raw eggs are as nutritious as cooked, how to ferment them, or describing mornings of a dozen or more.[15][16][17] Other members call the practice a meme.[18]

No studies found on egg yolk specifically for appearance outcomes such as skin or hair. Egg research that touches physique includes the whole-egg versus egg-white muscle protein synthesis trial in young men and the egg-breakfast weight-loss trial.[7][9] Wider egg research concerns cardiovascular risk, LDL cholesterol and allergy prevention in infants.[6][12][19]

lore.intro: Eggs come up on looksmax.org as a cheap staple, a source of energy and a raw-food experiment, and members disagree about whether they are an efficient protein source.[2][2][5]
